item.text: {"text":"[NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) uses residual stacks of dilated causal convolutions to expand history coverage without pooling. For stride-one layers, theoretical receptive-field width is 1 + Σ(k−1)d, counting every convolution; this describes reach, not demonstrated context use. [Effective receptive-field research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.04128) shows influence can concentrate within a smaller region. [ICLR 2024 activation-patching research](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/06a52a54c8ee03cd86771136bc91eb1f-Abstract-Conference.html) finds localization depends strongly on corruption method and measurement metric. These support diagnostic methods, but do not establish NextItNet-specific findings for 2024–2026.\n\nPractical adaptation: compare clean histories with matched replacements in lag bands, preserving length, occupied positions, recent suffix, and approximately item frequency. Keep the validation target and 99 unique negatives identical across interventions. Patch clean activations into corrupted runs at individual residual blocks and aligned positions; separately bypass residual branches to test necessity. Measure target-rank, target–negative score-margin, and HR@10 changes; report raw effects when normalized recovery has a near-zero denominator. Verify left-padding, final-nonpadding readout, causal isolation from future positions, and padding invariance before interpreting results. Avoid deletion-and-compaction interventions that shift surviving items. Include identity patches, interventions outside theoretical reach, and synthetic lag-dependent positive controls solely to validate probes. These are proposed adaptations, not published NextItNet results. Weak distant-history effects indicate limited measured sensitivity only after controls succeed; training-prefix effects establish sensitivity, while held-out validation assesses generalization. Keep one trained NextItNet model per category."}
